lesson.title: Nature's Dictionary: Reading the Genetic Code
lesson.summary: The genetic code is the complete set of rules mapping all sixty-four possible mRNA codons to an amino acid or a stop signal, a code that is redundant but never ambiguous, and nearly universal across life.
lesson.body:
With four possible bases read three at a time, an mRNA has sixty-four possible codons available to it. Of those sixty-four, sixty-one specify one of the twenty standard amino acids, and the remaining three, UAA, UAG, and UGA, are stop signals with no matching tRNA. Laid out completely, this full set of codon-to-amino-acid assignments is what biologists call the genetic code.

Because there are sixty-one codons available to specify only twenty amino acids, most amino acids end up with more than one codon that codes for them, a property called degeneracy or redundancy. Phenylalanine, for instance, is specified by both UUU and UUC, two different codons producing the exact same amino acid; these are called synonymous codons. It is worth being precise about what this redundancy does and does not mean. The genetic code is degenerate, meaning a given amino acid can often be reached by more than one codon, but it is not ambiguous, meaning a given codon never specifies more than one amino acid. UUU always means phenylalanine and nothing else; there is no codon in the standard genetic code that could be read as either one amino acid or another depending on circumstance. The redundancy runs one direction only, from amino acid to codon, never from codon to amino acid.

This redundancy is not spread evenly across a codon; it is concentrated almost entirely at the third position, which lines up with the wobble pairing described back in the chapter on tRNA structure. Because pairing at that third position can be looser than strict Watson-Crick pairing, a single tRNA anticodon can often recognize more than one synonymous codon, so a cell does not need sixty-one separate tRNAs to cover sixty-one sense codons.

One of the more striking features of this code is how broadly it is shared. With a handful of known exceptions, such as some differences in the code used by mitochondria and by certain single-celled organisms, virtually every organism on Earth, from bacteria to humans, uses the same codon assignments. A codon that specifies methionine in a human cell specifies methionine in a bacterial cell too. That near-universal sharing is strong evidence that all known life traces back to a common ancestor that already used this code, and it is also the practical reason genes from one species can often be read correctly when placed into the cells of a very different species.
